title: Made in Canada: Tracking Giants, Possibility and Failing in Public, with Amanda Lewis

host.name: Nola Simon
host.title: Futurist & Founder, Everyday Futurism
host.credentials: 17 years in cross-border insurance operations · Creator of the Assumption-Ground Audit

guest.name: Amanda Lewis
guest.title: Editor and author
guest.credentials: Edits legacy-creating books from Gabriola Island, British Columbia · Author of Tracking Giants

abstract: Amanda Lewis edits legacy-creating books from Gabriola Island, between Vancouver and Vancouver Island. When this was recorded, her book Tracking Giants, about searching for British Columbia's champion trees, was about to come out. The conversation covers the creative cycle of excitement, panic and reshaping, failing in public as an editor trained to get things right, why big trees grow big because of the forest around them, publishing as an ecosystem, leaving a publishing hub and watching an international client base grow, and workplaces built for real bodies.
takeaways: Name the creative cycle so you can keep going: get an idea, rush in, realize it is harder than it looks, panic, then reshape it into something doable.
Surface the value in failing in public. Amanda stopped blogging when the trees got hard to find, and friends told her the failing was the interesting part.
Map a book as part of an ecosystem: it has to live alongside your other work, and publishers look about two years ahead, so test whether the idea is evergreen or better as an article.
Interrogate the story that success requires a big city. Amanda's client base grew and became international after she moved to an island.
Run your days in chunks that match your energy, and treat the practices that help your career, like gardening, as seriously as the prestigious ones.

keyQA.question: What is a champion tree?
keyQA.answer: A champion is the largest tree of its species. In British Columbia they are listed by the BC Big Tree Registry at the University of British Columbia. Amanda Lewis set out to find them with no training, and learned quickly why forestry crews and mountaineers usually find them. When the pandemic hit, she shrank the project to the trees in her own backyard and neighbourhood.

keyQA.question: Why do champion trees grow so big?
keyQA.answer: The idea of a champion makes a tree look like it grows alone, but forests are interconnected, and the biggest trees grow big because of the forest around them. For Amanda, who tends to strive alone, the search got easier when she let people who knew what they were doing help.

keyQA.question: How do publishers decide whether an idea should be a book?
keyQA.answer: Amanda thinks of publishing as an ecosystem: a book has to live alongside your other offerings so your audience sees why you wrote it. Publishers are a bit like fortune tellers, looking about two years ahead, so a very new idea may be better as an article. The test is whether the idea is evergreen.

keyQA.question: Did leaving Toronto hurt Amanda Lewis's editing business?
keyQA.answer: No. She was afraid people would forget her if she left a publishing hub. She moved to Vancouver, then to Gabriola Island, and her client base grew and became international. One American client said her living on an island was part of why he hired her.
